pageTitle: Classical Guitar: The Art of Finger Mastery
subtitle: Master the art of traditional guitar technique and repertoire

introduction.title: Classical Guitar: The Art of Finger Mastery
introduction.text: The classical guitar is built around a single constraint that shapes everything else about it: the fingers, not a pick, generate the sound. That's why the neck is wider than a steel-string's, the strings are nylon rather than steel, and centuries of formal technique exist to govern exactly how each finger approaches the string. The result is an instrument capable of playing bass line, harmony, and melody simultaneously with a warmth and dynamic control that a pick simply can't produce.

columns.title: Classical Guitar Hallmarks
columns.text: Nylon strings exist because they're gentler on bare fingertips and produce a warmer, mellower tone than steel — a direct consequence of fingerstyle-only technique rather than an arbitrary design choice. The wider neck exists for the same reason: it gives four right-hand fingers and a thumb enough room to work independently across six strings, which is what makes the instrument's dense classical and flamenco repertoire playable in the first place.

cards.title: Classical Guitar
cards.description: Nylon strings under lower tension are what make the classical guitar comfortable to play fingerstyle for hours, and that same lower tension is why it can't project as loudly as a steel-string in a band setting — the trade-off for gentleness on the fingers is a quieter, more intimate voice best suited to solo performance.
items: Strings: Nylon (trebles) and wound nylon/silver (basses)
Neck: Wide (2" at nut), flat fretboard
Sound: Warm, mellow, intimate
Technique: Fingerstyle only, classical position
Repertoire: Classical, flamenco, bossa nova
Volume: Quieter, perfect for solo performance

cards.title: Steel-String Acoustic
cards.description: Steel strings under much higher tension are what give a steel-string acoustic its brighter, more projective voice, which is why it's the instrument of choice whenever a guitar needs to cut through a mix with other players rather than carry a piece on its own.
items: Strings: Steel core with bronze/phosphor bronze wrap
Neck: Narrower (1.75" typical), radiused fretboard
Sound: Bright, projective, cutting
Technique: Picks, strumming, various positions
Repertoire: Folk, country, rock, pop
Volume: Louder, cuts through band mix

cards.title: Construction Details
cards.description: Every construction choice on a classical guitar traces back to fingerstyle technique: nylon strings are kind to bare fingertips over long practice sessions, the wide flat fretboard gives four fingers room to work independently without a fretboard radius getting in the way, and the traditional tie-block bridge exists because nylon strings can't be anchored with ball-end pins the way steel strings are.
items: Nylon Strings: Gentle on fingers, warm tone, traditional sound
Wide Neck: Usually 2" at nut, accommodates fingerstyle technique
Flat Fretboard: No radius for classical playing position
Traditional Bridge: Tie-block system for string attachment

cards.title: Wood Selection
cards.description: Spruce and cedar dominate classical guitar tops for opposite reasons: spruce is stiffer and slower to open up but rewards a player with clarity and headroom as it ages, while cedar responds immediately with a warmer voice but has less ceiling for projection. Back and side woods add their own character on top of that — rosewood's density produces rich overtones, while cypress, prized in flamenco building, favors a brighter, more percussive attack that supports rhythmic playing over sustain.
items: Spruce Top: Most common, bright and responsive
Cedar Top: Warmer, immediate response, popular choice
Rosewood Back/Sides: Rich overtones, traditional choice
Cypress Back/Sides: Flamenco favorite, bright and percussive

cards.title: Traditional Posture
cards.description: The footstool-and-elevated-leg posture exists to bring the guitar up to a consistent angle and height regardless of the player's body size, which matters because classical technique depends on the right hand approaching the strings at a specific angle every time. Skip the posture and that angle drifts from note to note, which is what causes the inconsistent tone and technique plateaus that formal instruction is designed to prevent.

fields.label: Body Position
fields.value: Sit on front edge of chair; back straight, relaxed shoulders; left foot elevated on footstool; guitar rests on left thigh; guitar at 45-degree angle

fields.label: Hand Position
fields.value: Left thumb behind neck, not wrapped; right hand curved, fingers approach strings at angle; wrist straight, not bent; fingertips perpendicular to strings; relaxed, natural movement

cards.title: Modern Alternatives
cards.description: Many players now use guitar supports, cushions, or straps to achieve the proper playing angle without a footstool, reducing strain. The traditional footstool tilts the pelvis asymmetrically for long practice sessions, which is exactly the kind of repetitive strain that these newer supports were designed to eliminate while still achieving the same guitar angle.
items: Ergoplay or A-Frame supports
Cushions and pillows
Classical guitar straps
Adjustable height chairs

cards.title: Rest Stroke (Apoyando)
cards.description: Finger plucks through the string and rests on the next string, which channels more of the finger's energy directly into the string being played and produces a louder, more focused note than free stroke can. That extra volume and focus is why rest stroke is the default technique for single-note melodies and scales, where each note needs to project clearly above any accompanying texture.

fields.label: Benefits
fields.value: Powerful, focused tone; good for melodies; traditional technique

fields.label: Best Used For
fields.value: Scales, single-note passages, emphasized notes

cards.title: Free Stroke (Tirando)
cards.description: Finger plucks the string without touching adjacent strings, which is what makes it possible to sound multiple strings together rather than one at a time. That freedom to play several notes at once is why free stroke, not rest stroke, is the technique used for chords and arpeggios.

fields.label: Benefits
fields.value: Allows chord playing; lighter touch; more versatile

fields.label: Best Used For
fields.value: Arpeggios, chords, rapid passages

cards.title: Tremolo
cards.description: Rapid repetition of a single note with the a-m-i fingers, interleaved with a bass line played by the thumb, creates the illusion of a sustained melody line over accompaniment even though the guitar can't actually sustain a plucked note that long. That illusion of continuous melody is what makes tremolo pieces sound almost orchestral, which is why it became a signature device in Spanish Romantic repertoire.

fields.label: Benefits
fields.value: Creates sustained melody effect; beautiful classical sound; advanced expression

fields.label: Best Used For
fields.value: Romantic pieces, Spanish repertoire

cards.title: Rasgueado
cards.description: This flamenco strumming technique fans multiple fingers across the strings in rapid succession rather than plucking individually, producing a percussive, drum-like attack that a single-finger stroke can't replicate. That rhythmic drive is central to flamenco, where the guitar often functions as much as a rhythm instrument as a harmonic one.

fields.label: Benefits
fields.value: Percussive rhythm; flamenco authenticity; dynamic expression

fields.label: Best Used For
fields.value: Flamenco music, rhythmic accompaniment

cards.title: The Spanish Tradition
cards.description: Flamenco guitar shares the nylon-string construction of classical guitar but emphasizes rhythm, percussion, and passionate expression. Lower action lets the strings buzz slightly against the frets for a rawer, more percussive sound that classical technique deliberately avoids, and tap plates protect the top from the rhythmic finger-tapping (golpe) that would otherwise damage a classical guitar's finish over time.

fields.label: Flamenco Differences
fields.value: Lower string action for percussive effects; cypress back/sides for brighter tone; tap plates (golpeadores) to protect top; more aggressive playing style; emphasis on rhythm and passion

fields.label: Key Techniques
fields.value: Rasgueado (flamenco strumming); golpe (percussive tapping); alzapua (thumb technique); picado (fast scale passages); tremolo (rapid note repetition)

cards.title: Student ($200-800)
tableRows: Solid spruce top, perfect starter guitar

cards.title: Intermediate ($800-2500)
tableRows: Cedar top, Indian rosewood, excellent value

fields.label: Technique
fields.value: Proper posture and hand position; rest stroke and free stroke; basic scales and arpeggios; simple chord progressions

fields.label: Repertoire

fields.label: Advanced Technique
fields.value: Barre chords and advanced fingerings; tremolo technique; advanced arpeggios and scales; dynamic control and expression

fields.label: Intermediate Repertoire
fields.value: Sor studies and sonatinas; Bach lute suites (easier movements); Villa-Lobos Preludes; Spanish pieces (Tarrega)

fields.label: Advanced Skills
fields.value: Concert-level technique; extended techniques; interpretation and style; performance preparation

fields.label: Advanced Repertoire
fields.value: Major concertos (Rodrigo, etc.); complete Bach lute suites; modern masterworks; personal interpretation development

cards.title: Effective Practice
cards.description: Practicing slowly isn't a beginner's crutch, it's how the fingers learn the correct movement before speed gets added — practicing a mistake at full tempo just ingrains the mistake more efficiently. A metronome and honest recording serve the same purpose from different angles: both expose timing and tone problems that are nearly impossible to hear accurately while you're the one playing.
items: Slow practice: Build muscle memory correctly
Metronome use: Develop steady rhythm
Repetition: Perfect small sections before combining
Mental practice: Study scores away from guitar
Recording: Listen to your playing objectively

cards.title: Physical Wellness
cards.description: Classical technique demands a level of hand independence and sustained posture that builds real physical strain over time, which is why serious players treat warm-ups and posture breaks as non-negotiable rather than optional. Building endurance gradually rather than pushing through fatigue is what prevents the repetitive strain injuries that end up sidelining players who practice hard but ignore their body's signals.
items: Posture breaks: Avoid strain and injury
Hand exercises: Maintain flexibility
Gradual increase: Build endurance slowly
Proper warm-up: Scales and technical exercises
Relaxation: Stay loose and natural
